records.approved_Lodge_beginning: and that he gaue the king his surname,
records.editorial_rationale: Accept 'and that he gaue the king his surname' as the beginning of Lodge's transformed reporting clause, corresponding broadly to the Greek account in which the king's namesake tells him how he may see the gods. Lodge's formulation differs materially from Greek, Latin and Whiston. Do not silently correct 'gaue the king his surname' to the meaning of the Greek. Preserve the original TCP gaps within this passage.

original_proposal_record.anchor: and that he gaue the king his surname,
original_proposal_record.rationale: Greek and Latin say the king's namesake told him how to see the gods. Lodge instead writes 'and that he gaue the king his surname, that he might also see the gods', joining a naming clause to the advice. Propose the earlier 'and that he gaue' as Lodge's whole transformed reporting clause; the alternative begins only the explicit seeing-and-cleansing advice. Recommend the earlier proposal to preserve the reporting transition, while retaining the translation anomaly and TCP gaps without reconstruction.

records.approved_Lodge_beginning: and so opposed himselfe vnto the kings desire
records.editorial_rationale: Accept 'and so opposed himselfe vnto the kings desire' as the earliest counterpart to the Greek question about failing to oppose the king's desire to see the gods. Lodge combines this with the preceding question about foreseeing the prophet's death. Retain the overlap without rearranging the sentence.

original_proposal_record.anchor: and so opposed himselfe vnto the kings desire
original_proposal_record.rationale: Greek and Latin I.258 include the question about foreseeing the prophet's death, whereas I.259 begins the question about not immediately contradicting the king. Lodge fuses these into 'How chanced it then ... foresee his own death, and so opposed himselfe vnto the kings desire to see the gods?' Propose 'and so opposed' for the first I.259 counterpart; the alternative waits for the separate fear question, keeping the whole fused question in I.258. Recommend the earlier semantic seam inside the unchanged sentence. Whiston places both questions in its I.259, so it cannot determine this boundary.

Greek and Latin place their section boundary between the adjective describing purity and the noun denoting the commonwealth. Lodge reverses their order. Preserve Lodge's wording and the resulting non-isomorphic segmentation.

records.approved_Lodge_beginning: tyrant king, yet doth not he so feare him
records.editorial_rationale: Accept 'tyrant king, yet doth not he so feare him' as the earliest counterpart to the Greek opening δεσπότην. Latin and Whiston begin the corresponding section later, with the argument about the excellence of Jewish laws. Record the difference between the Greek-based and Latin/Whiston-based divisions. Preserve the marginal note immediately preceding this boundary in its original source position.

original_proposal_record.anchor: tyrant king, yet doth not he so feare him
original_proposal_record.rationale: Greek II.278 begins 'δεσπότην' (master), completing II.277's fear clause, before the argument from excellence of laws. Boysen and Whiston keep the ruler/fear clause in II.277 and begin II.278 at the excellence argument. Lodge writes 'where there is a tyrant king, yet doth not he so feare him ...; if therefore we do valorously endure'. Propose the earliest Greek counterpart, 'tyrant king', and retain the attached fear clause in II.278. The alternative at 'if therefore' follows Latin/Whiston. Recommend the principal Greek seam with explicit overlap; no words are moved, no duplicate or empty section is required, and no human approval is claimed.
